title: What Education Can Learn From Trusted Professions
author: Douglas Carnine
summary: Douglas Carnine argues that education remains in what he terms a 'period of preventable harm' — the interval between when evidence for effective practice was established and when it is uniformly enforced — because it lacks the five structural pillars that define trusted professions: a shared knowledge base, coherent preparation systems, competence-signaling licensure, quality-protecting accreditation, and accountability guardrails. Drawing lessons from medicine, maritime navigation, and finance, he shows that each of these professions exited its period of preventable harm not through internal professional agreement but through external pressure: legislative action, public scandal, regulatory enforcement. The parallels are disturbing in scale: the forty-year delay in universally requiring handwashing after Semmelweis's 1847 proof likely cost hundreds of thousands of lives; education's failure to mandate evidence-based reading instruction since 1970 has likely exposed 60 to 70 million fourth graders to preventable reading failure. In trusted professions, local control exists inside accountability guardrails — a hospital cannot declare itself exempt from sterile technique — but in education, local preference can simply override the strongest available evidence. Carnine's prescriptive conclusion is that the fifth pillar — accountability — is the master lever, and that State Departments of Education must evolve from passive data collectors to proactive enforcers with the authority to intervene when districts persistently fail to implement evidence-based instruction.
points: The 'period of preventable harm' framework reframes education's evidence gap not as a knowledge deficit but as a structural failure: the profession lacks the accountability guardrails that make departure from its knowledge base consequential rather than merely optional.

Historical parallels from medicine, maritime navigation, and finance share the same pattern — external pressure (legislative, legal, regulatory), not internal professional consensus, is what converts established evidence into mandated practice.

In trusted professions, local discretion exists inside accountability guardrails, not above them; education's error is allowing local preference to override professional knowledge entirely rather than operate within a shared evidence framework.

Education's scale makes its non-compliance uniquely damaging: with roughly 10 million educators and supporting professionals, the field has no reliable way even to measure how many practitioners deviate from evidence-based practices, unlike medicine or finance where imperfect compliance is at least visible and consequential.

An estimated 60-70 million fourth graders have experienced preventable reading failure since 1970 NAEP baselines, based on the gap between the current 40% 'Below Basic' rate and the 5-10% achievable with evidence-based instruction — a preventable injury in human terms, not merely an instructional shortcoming.
quotes: At present, education does not function as an evidence-aligned profession. That does not mean it lacks research, talented educators, or worthy intentions. It means the field has not yet built the accountability 'guardrails' needed to make reliable knowledge normal, expected, and enforceable in daily practice.
The period of preventable harm can be defined as the interval of time between when evidence was established and when evidence was uniformly applied by the profession.

In education, local preference too often overrides the strongest available evidence. A teacher may know what works, but the district may prohibit it. A principal may support sound instruction, but a board or superintendent may reverse it. A preparation program may improve, but local curriculum decisions may disconnect new teachers from what they learned.

A hospital cannot say, 'In our clinic, we do not believe in sterile technique.' An accounting office cannot say, 'We prefer not to follow accepted reporting standards.' A ship captain cannot say, 'Our local approach does not include standard navigation or safety procedures.'

The important point, however, is not that these professions have eliminated noncompliance. The important point is that they have built systems strong enough that the shared knowledge base still governs the field overall.

From the beginning of NAEP reading assessments in 1970 through 2024, the United States likely exposed roughly 60 to 70 million fourth graders to unnecessary serious reading failure, if one assumes that the current 'Below Basic' rate of about 40% could have been reduced to 5% to 10% through more effective evidence-based instruction.

That estimate is rough, but its implications are not. It suggests massive preventable harm in the form of reduced confidence, shame, frustration, and anxiety for children; heavy tutoring, advocacy, and emotional burdens for families.

Education still struggles to earn the same kind of trust that states extend to medicine, finance, and maritime work. Why? Effective support for educators and their students is lacking, which disempowers educators and causes widespread student failure.
